prompt: As countries try to reduce their carbon emissions, some argue that nuclear power must be part of the solution, while others believe that only renewable sources such as wind and solar should be developed. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
essay:
Both sides of this argument want the same grid: one that emits nothing and keeps the lights on. They disagree about how long the country is allowed to take getting there, and almost every other difference between them follows from that.

The renewables-only position is strongest over a long horizon. Wind and solar are now the cheapest generation ever built, their costs continue to fall while nuclear's stubbornly rise, and storage technologies that look inadequate today have a history of improving faster than forecast. Given thirty or forty years, a grid running on renewables with sufficient storage and interconnection is entirely plausible, and it would avoid both the waste problem and the small but genuinely dreadful tail risk of a serious accident. Nothing in the anti-nuclear case is unreasonable if that is the timescale.

The trouble is that emissions have to fall now, and over the next fifteen years the arithmetic changes completely. A grid that is mostly renewable still needs something to cover a windless fortnight in January, and at present the only options are storage that does not yet exist at that scale or gas that certainly does. This is why the practical choice is rarely nuclear against renewables; it is nuclear against gas, dressed up as a debate about renewables. Countries that closed reactors in the past two decades did not replace them with wind. They replaced them with coal and gas, and their emissions rose.

That is what settles it for me, though only for a period. Existing reactors should run as long as they are safe, and a modest programme of new ones is worth the cost and the unresolved waste question as insurance against the years when storage is still too small. But this is an argument for nuclear power as a bridge, not as a destination — and a bridge is only worth building if someone is seriously constructing the far bank while you cross.
title: Nuclear power in a low-carbon energy mix
